title: Papillon — the most famous escape ever written, and what the French files say
sources: Wikipedia: Henri Charrière — a Paris underworld figure nicknamed 'Papillon' after a butterfly tattoo on his chest; convicted in 1931 of murdering a pimp, which he always denied, and sentenced to life with hard labour; transported in 1933 to the penal colony at Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni, French Guiana; his 1969 book Papillon describes repeated escapes, life with an indigenous tribe in Colombia, solitary confinement, imprisonment on Devil's Island and a final escape in 1941 on a bag of coconuts riding the tide; he reached Venezuela, was freed in 1944–45, became a citizen and opened restaurants in Caracas and Maracaibo; the book sold over 1.5 million copies in France and was filmed in 1973 with Steve McQueen; he called it '75 percent true'; French records show he worked as a nursing assistant at the André-Bouron colonial hospital, where returning escapees told him their stories, and say he never served time on Devil's Island; Devil's Island has no towering cliffs but slopes gently into the sea; critics say the rescue of a guard's daughter from sharks was done by another convict, Alfred Steffen, who lost both legs; a French justice ministry report said the book 'should be divided by at least 10 to get near the truth'; in 2005, 104-year-old Charles Brunier, who also had a butterfly tattoo and was in the colony at the same time, claimed to be the real Papillon; Charrière was pardoned in 1970 and died in 1973.

Photos (public domain / CC0, Wikimedia Commons, Gallica/BnF): Henri Charrière (1971) and at his home in Caracas (1971); Devil's Island (1908) and the Îles du Salut (postcard); the penal colony at Saint-Laurent-du-Maroni; the convicts' hospital (1907); Le Petit Journal (1894); Charles Brunier
Film (public domain / CC0): US Virgin Islands coast, ocean surface waves, crashing waves (San Juan Islands), a thresher shark — illustrative, not French Guiana
Music: Satie, Gymnopédie No. 1, public domain

post.facebook:
Papillon — the most famous prison escape ever written: a man who floated away from Devil's Island on a sack of coconuts. But French records say he was never on Devil's Island at all.

Henri Charrière, a Paris crook nicknamed Papillon after the butterfly tattooed on his chest, got life for murder in 1931 and always said he was innocent. He was shipped to the penal colony of French Guiana. In his book he escapes again and again, lives with a tribe in Colombia, survives solitary, ends up on Devil's Island and finally rides the tide away on a sack of coconuts, reaching Venezuela. The book sold over 1.5 million copies in France and became a Hollywood film with Steve McQueen.

But the prison files say he worked in the colony hospital, where escaped convicts told him their stories. Devil's Island has no famous cliffs — it slopes gently into the sea. Critics say even his rescue of a girl from sharks was another convict's deed. A French ministry report said to divide his story by ten to get near the truth; Charrière said it was 75 percent true. And in 2005, 104-year-old Charles Brunier said he was the real Papillon — butterfly tattoo and all.

So whose escape was it? 👇

youtube.description:
Papillon — the most famous prison escape ever written. But French records say Henri Charrière was never on Devil's Island at all.

Charrière, nicknamed Papillon after his butterfly tattoo, was sentenced to life in 1931 and sent to the penal colony of French Guiana. His 1969 bestseller (and the 1973 film with Steve McQueen) describes escapes, solitary confinement and a final getaway from Devil's Island on a sack of coconuts. French records tell another story: he worked as a nursing assistant in the colony hospital, hearing other convicts' tales, and never served on Devil's Island. A ministry report said his book should be 'divided by ten'; he called it 75% true. In 2005, 104-year-old Charles Brunier claimed to be the real Papillon.
